{{Short description|Theorem in geometric number theory}}
In mathematics, '''Minkowski's second theorem''' is a result in the [[geometry of numbers]] about the values taken by a [[Normed vector space|norm]] on a lattice and the volume of its fundamental cell. It is named so because it is a strengthening of [[Minkowski's theorem]].

==Setting==
Let {{mvar|K}} be a [[closed set|closed]] [[convex set|convex]] [[central symmetry|centrally symmetric]] body of positive finite volume in {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^n</math>.  The ''gauge''<ref>Siegel (1989) p.6</ref> or ''distance''<ref>Cassels (1957) p.154</ref><ref>Cassels (1971) p.103</ref> [[Minkowski functional]] {{math|''g''}} attached to {{math|''K''}} is defined by
<math display="block">g(x) = \inf \left\{\lambda \in \mathbb{R} : x \in \lambda K \right\} . </math>

Conversely, given a norm {{math|''g''}} on <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^n</math> we define {{mvar|K}} to be
<math display="block">K = \left\{ x \in \R^n : g(x) \le 1 \right\} . </math>

Let {{math|Γ}} be a [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] in <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^n</math>.  The '''successive minima''' of {{mvar|K}} or {{math|''g''}} on {{math|Γ}} are defined by setting the {{mvar|k}}-th successive minimum {{math|''λ<sub>k</sub>''}} to be the [[infimum]] of the numbers  {{math|''λ''}} such that {{math|''λK''}} contains {{mvar|k}} linearly-independent vectors of {{math|Γ}}.  We have {{math|0 < ''λ''<sub>1</sub> ≤ ''λ''<sub>2</sub> ≤ ... ≤ ''λ<sub>n</sub>'' < ∞}}.

==Statement==
The successive minima satisfy<ref>Cassels (1957) p.156</ref><ref>Cassels (1971) p.203</ref><ref>Siegel (1989) p.57</ref>
<math display="block">\frac{2^n}{n!} \operatorname{vol}\left(\mathbb{R}^n/\Gamma\right) \le \lambda_1\lambda_2\cdots\lambda_n \operatorname{vol}(K)\le 2^n \operatorname{vol}\left(\mathbb{R}^n/\Gamma\right).</math>

== Proof ==
A basis of linearly independent lattice vectors {{math| ''b''<sub>1</sub>, ''b''<sub>2</sub>, ..., ''b<sub>n</sub>''}} can be defined by {{math|1=''g''(''b<sub>j</sub>'') = ''λ<sub>j</sub>''}} (warning : it may be not a basis of the lattice, but only a basis of the [[Ambient space (mathematics)|ambient space]]).

The lower bound is proved by considering the convex [[polytope]] {{math|2''n''}} with vertices at {{math|±''b''<sub>''j''</sub>/ ''λ<sub>j</sub>''}}, which has an interior enclosed by {{mvar|K}} and a volume which is {{math|2<sup>''n''</sup> / (''n''! ''λ''<sub>1</sub>''λ''<sub>2</sub>...''λ''<sub>''n''</sub>)}} times an integer multiple of a [[primitive cell]] of the lattice (as seen by scaling the polytope by {{math|''λ<sub>j</sub>''}}  along each basis vector to obtain {{math|2<sup>''n''</sup>}} [[Simplex|{{mvar|n}}-simplices]] with lattice point vectors), the integer being the index of the <math>\mathbb{Z}</math>-span of the family <math>(b_i)_i</math> as a subgroup of the lattice.

To prove the upper bound, consider functions {{math|''f<sub>j</sub>''(''x'')}} sending points {{mvar|x}} in <math display="inline">K </math> to the centroid of the subset of points in <math display="inline">K </math> that can be written as <math display="inline">x + \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} a_i b_i </math> for some real numbers <math display="inline"> a_i </math>. Then the coordinate transform <math display="block">x' = h(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (\lambda_i -\lambda_{i-1}) f_i(x)/2 </math> has a Jacobian determinant <math display="inline">J = \lambda_1 \lambda_2 \ldots \lambda_n/2^n </math>. If <math display="inline">p </math> and <math display="inline">q </math> are in the [[Interior (topology)|interior]] of  <math display="inline">K </math> and <math display="inline">p-q = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i b_i </math>(with <math display="inline">a_k \neq 0 </math>) then <math display="block">(h(p) - h(q)) = \sum_{i=0}^k c_i b_i \in \lambda_k K </math> with <math display="inline">c_k = \lambda_k a_k /2 </math>, where the inclusion in <math display="inline">\lambda_k K </math> (specifically the interior of <math display="inline">\lambda_k K </math>) is due to convexity and symmetry. But lattice points in the interior  of <math display="inline">\lambda_k K </math> are, by definition of <math display="inline">\lambda_k </math>, always expressible as a linear combination of <math display="inline">b_1, b_2, \ldots b_{k-1} </math>, so any two distinct points of <math display="inline">K' = h(K) = \{ x' \mid h(x) = x' \} </math> cannot be separated by a lattice vector.

The entire space <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is tiled by translated copies of a primitve cell <math display="inline">\mathbb{R}^n = \bigcup_{v \in \Gamma} \bigl((\mathbb{R}^n / \Gamma) + v\bigr)</math>. The intersections <math display="inline">K'_v := K' \cap \bigl((\mathbb{R}^n / \Gamma) + v\bigr)</math> with <math display="inline">K'</math> have a total volume in sum that is less than the volume of a single primite cell <math>\mathbb{R}^n / \Gamma</math> and therefore <math display="block">\operatorname{vol} (K) \cdot J = \operatorname{vol}(K') \le \operatorname{vol}(\R^n/\Gamma). </math>To see this, consider two intersections <math display="inline">K'_u</math> and <math display="inline">K'_v</math> with <math display="inline">u, v \in \Gamma</math> and their translated versions <math display="inline">K'_u - u</math> and <math display="inline">K'_v - v</math> that are both contained in the primitive cell located at the origin. If they would intersect at some point <math display="inline">y \in (\mathbb{R}^n / \Gamma)</math>, then the two original points <math display="inline">y + u \in K'_u \subseteq K'</math> and <math display="inline">y + v \in K'_v \subseteq K'</math> would be separated by a lattice vector, which can be seen by considering the difference <math display="inline">(y + u) - (y + v) = u - v \in \Gamma</math>. This cannot be the case and therefore, translating every of the intersections into the primitive cell located at the origin does not lead to any intersections, which shows the claim.
